_note: Quiz and true-or-false items written but not yet blind-checked; apply_check.py moves checked items onto the site.

item.statement: Quitting smoking after 55 is too late to make any difference.
item.why: In a big US study, people who stopped at 55 to 64 gained roughly 4 years compared with people who kept smoking. That's a group average.

item.statement: Quitting smoking by 40 wipes out all the extra risk of dying early.
item.why: In a big US study, people who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept smoking.

item.statement: Nicotine gum and patches hook people as much as smoking does.
item.why: A big US report says nicotine medicines carry a low risk of getting hooked. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

item.statement: It's been proven that nicotine on its own causes cancer.
item.why: A big US report found the evidence too thin to say either way. It says burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm.

item.statement: Breathing other people's smoke has been linked to sudden infant death.
item.why: A 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence to call it a cause. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

item.statement: After smoke-free laws came in, heart attacks fell in people under 65.
item.why: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence for fewer heart attacks and similar events in people under 65. That's the report's judgment, second-hand.

item.statement: If you don't inhale, cigars don't raise your risk of mouth cancer.
item.why: In one big old US study, people who said they didn't inhale still died more often of mouth, gullet and voice-box cancer than people who never smoked. A second study had too few to be sure.

item.statement: Swedish snus has been shown to raise the risk of mouth cancer.
item.why: In an independent review, mouth cancer showed no clear difference between men who used snus and men who used no tobacco. A cancer agency's verdict covers all smokeless tobacco, not snus alone.

item.statement: Snus has been linked to cancer of the gullet.
item.why: An independent review estimated about 55 cases in 100,000 men who used snus, against 16 in men who used no tobacco. This can't show snus caused it.

item.statement: Nicotine pouches have been shown to be safe in long-term studies.
item.why: No study has followed people who use pouches for more than 6 months, or looked at disease or death.

item.statement: The label on nicotine pouches always tells you how strong they are.
item.why: In a German lab's test of 44 pouches bought in 2021, only 15 printed the nicotine in milligrams, and 4 gave no sign of strength at all.

item.statement: A nicotine patch plus gum helped more people quit than one alone.
item.why: In 16 trials, about 17 in 100 quit for 6 months or more with both, against 14 in 100 with one kind. The gain is small.

item.statement: Skin problems from nicotine patches are rare.
item.why: In one source a review cites, up to 54 in 100 people had skin irritation from patches, usually mild.

item.statement: Chest pain or a pounding heart was no more common on nicotine patches and gum.
item.why: In 15 trials, it came up in 2.5 in 100 people using them, against 1.4 in 100 on a dummy or nothing. Serious problems were too rare to compare.

item.statement: In trials, nicotine vapes helped more people quit smoking than patches or gum.
item.why: In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more with a vape. More people kept vaping, and effects over years aren't known.

item.statement: Simply advising people who smoke to vape helps them quit.
item.why: In 2 trials, advice to vape without giving a vape made no clear difference. Being given a vape did better, but those trials couldn't hide who got one.

item.statement: NAC pills have been shown to stop hangovers.
item.why: In the one trial, 49 young adults' next-morning hangovers weren't clearly different on NAC than on dummy pills. One small trial can't rule out an effect, either.

item.statement: A hangover is just being dried out, so drinking water fixes it.
item.why: Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, while the hangover lasted all day. And up to mid-2024, no experiment had tested water as a fix.

item.statement: Trials show that teaching students safer drinking habits cuts how much they drink.
item.why: In 15 trials, mostly with US students, how much they said they drank didn't clearly change. No trial tested one habit alone.

item.statement: Students drank more on days they had a designated driver.
item.why: In two day-by-day studies, they drank more and had more problems on those days. The author thinks people plan a ride home for heavy nights.

item.statement: People most often say accepting a hard trip, or calming the mind, is what helped.
item.why: Two surveys agree. In one, 85 in 100 found letting go helpful. These are memories, and no study tested any of it.

item.statement: Harm reduction habits have been shown to prevent bad trips.
item.why: In the one survey that measured both, a higher safety-habit score went only with a slightly easier first trip, not the latest. People recalled it all at once, often years later.

item.statement: A bedtime routine got most kids on ADHD medicine to sleep within an hour.
item.why: In one study, only 5 of about 28 children did, though on average they fell asleep sooner: 69 minutes, down from 92. There was no comparison group.

item.statement: In quit-smoking trials, vapes clearly did more serious harm than patches or gum.
item.why: No clear difference showed up: 7 against 6 in 100 had serious problems. But problems were few, and the trials lasted about 2 years at most, too short to show rare or later harms.

item.statement: Trials show that nicotine pouches help people quit smoking.
item.why: Nobody knows yet: four small trials of 8 weeks at most couldn't tell. Three of them took people who weren't planning to quit.

item.statement: If you vape, you take in as many harmful chemicals as if you smoked.
item.why: Much less of most: in a US survey, about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical, though nicotine wasn't clearly lower. These are chemical levels, not illness.

item.statement: Vaping as well as smoking cuts the smoke chemicals in your body.
item.why: In a US survey, people who both vaped and smoked had as much as people who only smoked, or more, at about the same number of cigarettes a day.

item.statement: Studies have shown that vaping causes heart disease.
item.why: Nobody can say yet. In a big US study, people who only vaped had no clear rise in heart disease over 4 years at most, but only 41 of them got it: too few to be sure either way.

item.statement: Most adults who vape every day, and don't smoke, say they feel dependent.
item.why: In a US survey, 77 in 100 adults who only vaped daily said so, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily. The survey is from 2013 to 2014, and nearly all had smoked before.

item.statement: People who vape daily feel just as addicted as people who smoke daily.
item.why: Fewer reported signs of dependence in a US survey: 73 in 100 adults who only vaped daily had strong cravings, against 87 in 100 who only smoked daily. It's what people said, and nearly all who vaped had smoked before.

item.statement: Vaping indoors leaves the air as clean as before.
item.why: Studies found more nicotine and tiny particles in the air, though less than with cigarette smoke. None of the studies we read checked whether that harms people nearby.

item.statement: The famous figure that vaping is 95% less harmful comes from long-term health studies.
item.why: No study we read tracked illness or death for years in people who only vape against people who smoke. Critics say the figure began as the views of 12 people at one meeting in 2013; a UK review says it still broadly fits the short and medium term.

item.statement: In studies, a short walk eased the urge to smoke, compared with sitting still.
item.why: In 19 small trials, the urge was about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale right afterwards. It was rated only minutes later, and people knew they'd exercised.

item.statement: In trials, people on nicotine gum and the like felt less grumpy in their first week off smoking.
item.why: All 9 trials that checked found less grumpiness in the first week than with a dummy version. The review gave no sizes, and a drug company paid for it.
